It is not the advantage of a reduction, because a reduction fixed in advance could hard-code a failing pair.

Proof sketch. The proof has four main parts, stated as lemmas in §C.3.

  1. PQXDH (Lemma 1) bounds the key indistinguishability of HroH_{\mathrm{ro}}Hro​ by βKIδ\beta_{\mathsf{KI}}^{\delta}βKIδ​. Its proof is a sequence of game hops in the style of [52].

  2. Single session (Lemma 2) bounds the advantage of an adversary against one ratchet session, started from a uniform key, by Sess\mathsf{Sess}Sess.

  3. Composition (Lemma 3) reduces the game run on the model to the key indistinguishability of the handshake and to one single-session game per promoted session, by a hybrid argument over the sessions.

  4. Refinement (Lemma 4) states that every run of the executable has the model’s outcome, unless the machine runs out of memory. Its proof is compositional, in a separation logic for AArch64. Each compiled function, from musl’s start-up code and its mallocng allocator through the CLI, protobuf, libsignal and SPQR, gets a contract that relates its registers and memory to the corresponding model function. The contracts are proved by symbolic execution. The lemma holds for every placement of the code in memory that matches the executable, so addresses and relocations are checked against its bytes rather than trusted from the linker.

The theorem follows from the four lemmas by coupling the two games. The game on the executable stores directories where the game on the model stores model states, and the coupling maintains that each directory is the encoding of the corresponding state. By Lemma 4, together with a proof that no run in the game exhausts memory (§4.1), this invariant breaks only if a Kyber1024 decapsulation fails in an honest handshake, which gives the δkem\delta_{\mathrm{kem}}δkem​ term. Otherwise, the adversary wins both games with the same probability. ML-KEM-768 decryption failures in SPQR are charged once for the whole game: the Lean proof carries out the composition in a game that stops at the first such failure and bounds the probability of reaching it by 2 εmlkem(A)2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mlkem}}(A)2εmlkem​(A).

5.2.4 Assumptions and Idealizations

Cryptographic assumptions. All but two of our assumptions are standard. The two exceptions arise because libsignal uses each party’s long-term Curve25519 secret key for two purposes: to compute X25519 Diffie-Hellman shared secrets in the handshake, and to sign the party’s prekeys with XEdDSA. Standard assumptions treat each primitive on its own, with its own key, and say nothing about whether using one key for both could help an attacker. For example, signatures on chosen messages might help it compute DH secrets, or DH results might help it forge signatures. We therefore use joint-security assumptions [46, 95]: XEdDSA signatures remain unforgeable even for an attacker that can also obtain DH results for the same key, and Gap-DH remains hard even for an attacker that can also obtain signatures under it.

Outside the trusted base, we prove in Lean that both joint assumptions reduce to standard Gap-DH when SHA-512 is modeled as a random oracle (§C.10). The main theorem keeps the joint assumptions, because deriving them from Gap-DH would weaken the bound considerably. Finally, ML-KEM-768 decryption failures are not covered by an assumption; the bound charges them directly as εmlkem(A)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mlkem}}(A)εmlkem​(A) (§5.2.3).

Random oracle. Clause 2 of the theorem treats the handshake’s HKDF as a random oracle. This is a heuristic: real HKDF is a fixed function, so clause 2 is not a theorem about it. Clause 1 makes no such idealization, and none of the ratchet’s key derivations are idealized in either clause.

Environment. The routines that libsignal-cli calls through contracts (§4) are assumed to behave as their Lean specifications say. The theorem also assumes functional properties of the primitives, such as that decryption inverts encryption, and fixes features of the process environment, such as the clock, the kernel’s random bytes, the stack size and the available memory (§4.1). §C.5 lists these assumptions. Running out of memory is not assumed away: a proof shows that no run in the game exhausts the available memory (§4.1).

5.2.5 Limitations

Our bounds give no guarantee against a quantum adversary. The symbolic proof covers part of this gap (§5.1). The game also restricts the adversary in ways that the literature does not. The most significant restriction is that the adversary cannot inject its own PQXDH initial message to the responder of a session that is later promoted. Further, the theorem does not cover the privacy of the payload, or the authentication of the responder, for first messages of handshakes that are never promoted. As in ACD19, corruption is refused at some points, for instance while an uncompromised message is in transit. Our game also refuses it until the initiator reaches epoch 10, since until then she may still hold the receiving chain for the leaked signed prekey.

The setting is simplified as well. Each promotion starts one session, messages have a fixed length, and there is no multi-device state. Identity keys are trusted on first use. The statistical terms limit the bound to moderate scale: if nearly every message starts a new epoch, they make it vacuous for single sessions of about 25,00025{,}00025,000 messages, or for 2202^{20}220 sessions of 2102^{10}210 messages.

We note that tightening bounds like this is a natural task for AI. Because the theorem’s statement is a Lean definition, a tighter bound is a change to the specification, which humans review, followed by a new proof campaign, which agents carry out.

Finally, the results concern our build of libsignal-cli, run as a fresh process on a machine with the memory of §4.1, not Signal’s own applications, and some of the environment assumptions are argued informally. §C.6 lists the remaining restrictions.

5.3 Trusted Computing Base

The trusted computing base (TCB) is the code that must be audited in order to have confidence that the theorems provide the security guarantees that we claim. To believe our theorems, a reader must check their statements and, transitively, every definition they use. For the symbolic proof, this is the DyLean model and its security statements, the event layer, the concretization function γ\gammaγ, the refinement statement with its collision clause, and the environment’s restrictions (§5.1.6). The computational proof trusts the definitions of the game, the assumption games and the bound, the Lean model of libsignal and SPQR, and the random-oracle step (§5.2.4).

Both proofs trust (a) the AArch64 semantics and the Lean model of how Linux runs a process (§2.2, §4.1), (b) the contracts of the hooked routines (§4), and (c) the functional and algebraic properties assumed of the cryptographic primitives. These are definitions that are transitively included in the theorem statements. The TCB also includes the tooling that extracts symbol names from the compiler’s object files, and the scripts that build the binary in a reproducible way (§C.6).

Everything else is checked by Lean, including the model-level proofs, the refinement, preservation and coupling arguments, the game hops and reductions, the function contracts and the program logic. For this reason, trusting our proofs also requires trusting Lean itself. The Lean community has invested significantly in trustworthiness of the Lean system, including the design of a small, carefully audited kernel, as well as independent kernels and consistency proofs [36, 37, 16]. Notably, however, the Rust compiler is not trusted. An error in any of the untrusted components that compromises the security properties that we formalize, including a bug in the compiler, or a bug in the Rust code, would cause the theorems to become false, so that the proof would fail.

6 Finding Historical Bugs

To check whether our specifications are strong enough to catch real bugs, we reintroduced two bugs that Cheval et al. [40] found in libsignal and that are now fixed. We injected each bug by reverse-applying its upstream fix commit to the libsignal v0.105.4 source and recompiling the binary, which we call Asmbug\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}}Asmbug​.

  • Weak state [40, §3.2.1], fix cd36118: a prekey message that fails to decrypt on its new session is trial-decrypted with older sessions, and if that succeeds the new session’s unconfirmed state, which holds a copy of the signed prekey secret, is stored.

  • Small subgroup [40, §3.2.2], fix 5293caa: the PQXDH responder does not check that the initiator’s X25519 base key is torsion-free and in range, so a replayed handshake with a mangled base key creates a second session with the same shared secret.

For both bugs we have complete Lean proofs that the symbolic security theorem (§5.1.4) does not hold of the bug-injected binary, ¬Sec(Asmbug)\neg\mathrm{Sec}(\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}})¬Sec(Asmbug​). Recall that Sec(Asm)\mathrm{Sec}(\mathit{Asm})Sec(Asm) requires that, for every extern interpretation I\mathcal{I}I meeting the contracts and every well-formed setup rrr, there exist opaque-symbol byte functions SSS such that every collision-free hardware trace τ∈TracesI,W(r)\tau \in \mathrm{Traces}_{\mathcal{I},W}(r)τ∈TracesI,W​(r) is explained by at least one reachable model trace (Expl(τ)≠∅\mathrm{Expl}(\tau) \neq \emptysetExpl(τ)=∅) and satisfies all ten security queries of Table 2 on every such explanation. Each disproof exhibits concrete witness inputs and splits into two parts: a specification part showing that, under a valid extern interpretation I\mathcal{I}I and well-formed setup rrr, no choice of SSS either explains the resulting hardware trace τ\tauτ, which has fresh coins, in the model or excuses it as a collision; and an implementation part showing that Asmbug\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}}Asmbug​ produces τ\tauτ under the AArch64 semantics (§2.2).

For the small-subgroup bug, Alice initiates a session and sends a prekey message whose X25519 base key the attacker modifies by setting bit 255, giving a distinct encoding with the same Diffie-Hellman outputs; the model’s canonical-key check rejects this message, whereas Asmbug\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}}Asmbug​ accepts it and stores a session. For the weak-state bug, Alice establishes a session with Bob (leaving skipped message keys in Bob’s session file) and then initiates a second session; the attacker splices the second session’s PQXDH header onto an inner message from the first session, which Asmbug\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}}Asmbug​ accepts via trial decryption against the stored session while no model transition explains the run. Both disproofs need no assumptions beyond Lean’s standard axioms: the Lean kernel parses the SHA-256-pinned ELF binary Asmbug\mathit{Asm}_{\mathrm{bug}}Asmbug​ and steps its AArch64 machine code across the runs of each witness trace.

On the other hand, refuting the computational theorem is much harder. The theorem states that there exist cost-bounded reductions, against hardness assumptions such as Gap Diffie-Hellman, whose success probabilities bound the advantage of every adversary. To refute it, one must exhibit an adversary that exploits the bug for which every cost-bounded reduction rarely succeeds, which amounts to proving the hardness assumptions themselves, an open problem.

7 AlphaProof Code in Practice

We now describe how we used AlphaProof Code in our verification of libsignal. The proof work was done by a team of five over four weeks, working in parallel on symbolic and computational proofs. Each of us ran agents nonstop on our own workstation, directing specification work and launching proof campaigns on different parts of the system.

Scale. The repository contains nearly 7 million lines of Lean, counting comments and blank lines. About 6.5 million of them are proofs: 5.3 million about the binary, which both security proofs share, about 860,000 for the computational proof and about 350,000 for the symbolic proof. Another 140,000 lines prove the reintroduced bugs (§6), and 70,000 verify the allocator. The verified libsignal code is about 560 KB, about 140,000 AArch64 instructions. The specification directories hold about 54,000 lines, but only part of them is trusted: every file is marked as trusted, trusted in part, or checked by Lean. Reading every definition that our headline theorems depend on means reading about 18,000 lines of code in the repository (about 28,000 with documentation), plus about 8,000 lines of the AArch64 semantics and a Lean representation of the compiled machine code (about 95,000 lines), which a tool extracts from the compiler’s object files; Lean checks its code against the executable’s bytes, so only the symbol names it assigns need to be trusted.

Writing specifications. The most important lesson from our experience is that, once proofs become cheap, the hard question is what to prove. The majority of our effort went not into proofs but into specifications. This trend is perhaps apparent in software development more broadly, but it is particularly acute for cryptographic protocols, where an entire literature is devoted to the question of how to formalize security (§8). One possible future is that programmers write formal security specifications, natural-language intent and performance constraints, and AI generates, optimizes and proves the implementation.

Our specifications were developed through an intense back-and-forth between humans and agents powered by Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5. For each component—for example, the binary contracts of a libsignal entry point, or the computational main theorem—the specification writer drafted a small set of top-level statements, following a model from the literature where one existed. An agent from a different model family then reviewed the draft for faithfulness to the source paper and to libsignal, for strength (would it rule out known or plausible bugs?), and, where it goes beyond the literature, for consistency with the literature’s conventions. We gave many rounds of targeted feedback before approving a specification and pinning it as the target for proofs. Left to themselves, agents produced specifications that were hard to audit; we sometimes directed rewrites for legibility, which paid off when new team members joined late to review them.

Writing specifications against real code also turned out to be a stress test for the literature. For both formalizations we record every place where the Lean statements depart from their reference papers or from libsignal, together with its effect on the result; the computational catalog has over 200 entries and the symbolic one about 35. Most are routine: the same idea stated differently in Lean, a place where libsignal differs from the scheme analyzed on paper, or a restriction the papers needed for their tools to terminate, which our symbolic model lifts. Some, however, are errors in the published analyses that we had to repair before the proofs could go through. Fifteen are gaps or bugs in the computational analysis of the Double Ratchet [7], such as missing hypotheses and security game conditions that allow trivial wins. On the symbolic side, the printed ProVerif queries of Cheval, Jacomme and Richards [40] look up skipped message keys at the wrong ratchet index, which makes receiver-side forward secrecy false as printed, leave a variable unbound, and bracket post-compromise security so that exposing a party’s own DH key, together with any root-key compromise, excuses a message regardless of when the heal happened. In the PQXDH analysis of Bhargavan et al. [28], reading “some SPKB\mathsf{SPK}_BSPKB​ was compromised” literally makes the session-independence corollary unprovable; we bind it to the session’s own signed prekey, as their ProVerif query does.

Generating proofs. The proofs were produced entirely by agent teams powered by Gemini 4 Carbon (§2.3), and none of the authors wrote any proof code. Keeping dozens of agents productive for days at a time is an engineering problem in its own right, and much of our early effort went into the skills that define the agent team. We developed them iteratively by watching campaigns run. A separate agent, above the team orchestrator, serves only as the interface between us and the team: it monitors the team, and we used its logs together with it to diagnose bottlenecks and propose fixes to its processes. Early on, monitoring the team took a lot of human time; this dropped as the skills matured. In the near future, we expect teams like this one to improve themselves.

We summarize a few improvements that emerged through human-AI iterative co-evolution in this way. Agents share notices through a common bulletin file rather than repeating messages. Team leads try to refute their goals before assigning work, fix shared parameters such as stack bounds across callees, and point workers to existing lemmas. Support agents batch expensive Lean builds to fit in memory, watch for stalled agents and exhausted model quotas, and refactor slow modules. The orchestrator reshapes the team as the campaign evolves. Every new invariant an agent introduces must come with a witness that it holds on some reachable state, so that agents cannot make progress by proving vacuous lemmas.

While no human wrote proof code, compute latency was an issue. A clean build of our proofs could take several hours, and early in the project, small source changes or a recompiled binary required large proof repairs. Better program-semantics infrastructure later reduced this. We see substantial room for optimization of proofs generated by and proof techniques deployed by AI.

Preventing specification weakening. Agents under pressure to finish a goal will sometimes weaken it [107, 78], for example by adding a hypothesis or narrowing a precondition, and this can happen indirectly through a definition that the statement depends on: in one swarm of Lean-proving agents, an agent redefined a predicate used in a conjecture’s hypothesis as False, and the trick spread to the rest of the swarm [78]. We therefore never rely on an agent’s own report that a goal is done. The gatekeeper (§2.4) sees only file paths and theorem names, and none of the provers’ dialogue or explanations; Lean replays every proof in a fresh environment, and sorry and native_decide are rejected.

At the same time, freezing the first draft of a specification is too rigid. Even experienced specification writers rarely get every detail right on the first try, and first drafts are often overly conservative in benign ways that make them false of the real code. Our solution is the amendment process of §2.3. An amendment is allowed only if the proof cannot instead be completed with a stronger invariant or a different decomposition, and only if it keeps the non-vacuity witnesses and honest runs covered. A neutral amendment must bring the specification closer to the code. A proposal that would weaken security to match the code is never accepted as an amendment; it is raised to a human as a potential bug. Accepted amendments are small and logged with their justification on an audited branch. Amendments that change trusted assumptions are approved during the campaign, by one of us or under a policy we set (§2.3), and all amendments are reviewed by us at the end of each campaign. One example is extending the composed symbolic query’s handshake-compromise exception from the initial root key to the initial chain key derived alongside it.

The human role. To summarize, we decided the scope and order of the work, chose the reference models, and guided and approved the trusted statements. We also designed the structure of the specifications and guided the overall proof strategy: for example, writing reductions in a small reduction language with a cost semantics (§5.2.2), and, for the symbolic proof, an event layer and concretization homomorphism that maps binary executions to protocol events, together with a refinement to a DyLean model up to collisions that preserves the security properties (§5.1.4). During proof campaigns, we reviewed escalated specification issues and potential bugs, adjudicated amendments that change trusted assumptions, and monitored progress through status logs. We also designed the skills that define the agent team, and refined them as we observed the agents’ behavior. We did not write proofs. Every statement we present as a theorem is checked by Lean, and every assumption we rely on is listed among the trusted definitions (§5.3).

8 Related Work

Analyses of the Signal protocol design. Kobeissi, Bhargavan and Blanchet [67] analyzed a variant of Signal with ProVerif and CryptoVerif. Bhargavan et al. [28] verified PQXDH with ProVerif and CryptoVerif, finding issues in an early version of its specification. Cheval, Jacomme and Richards [40] gave an automated analysis of the Double Ratchet composed with PQXDH, found the two libsignal bugs we re-inject in §6, and proved forward secrecy and post-compromise security. Our symbolic theorems restate theirs and those of Bhargavan et al. with adaptation to connect to our libsignal-cli binary.

On the computational side, Cohn-Gordon et al. [42, 43] gave the first game-based analysis of Signal’s X3DH handshake and Double Ratchet as a multi-stage key exchange. Alwen, Coretti and Dodis [7] defined secure messaging with immediate decryption and proved the Double Ratchet secure in a modular way. Our ratchet game follows their definitions.

Fiedler and Günther [52] analyzed PQXDH in a key-indistinguishability game, which our handshake oracles follow. Both Fiedler and Günther [52] and Bhargavan et al. [28] give each party separate Diffie-Hellman and signing identity keys; Lemma 1 bounds the one-key handshake of libsignal under joint X25519 Gap-DH and XEdDSA unforgeability assumptions [46, 95, 35], while standalone Lean proofs for the two-key key-indistinguishability and first-message authentication models remain in the artifact outside the trusted base.

Verified protocol implementations. Several projects verify implementations rather than designs. miTLS and Project Everest [27] implemented TLS in F#\## and proved computational security of the implementation, Noise⋆^\star⋆ [59] generates verified implementations of Noise protocols, and LibSignal⋆^\star⋆ [83] is a verified implementation of the Signal protocol written in F⋆^\star⋆ and compiled to WebAssembly. These are new implementations written for verification; LibSignal⋆^\star⋆, in particular, is separate from the production libsignal.

Deployed code has been verified for narrower properties: the s2n TLS library is continuously verified with SAW [41] for functional correctness of its HMAC, DRBG and handshake state machine, and SPQR’s production Rust crate is proved panic-free with hax [25, 90], alongside ProVerif models of its design [89]. Neither proves protocol-level security of the code. One line of work extracts a model from implementation code and verifies the model: fs2pv [26] translates F# code into ProVerif models, Aizatulin et al. [2] extract ProVerif models from C code by symbolic execution, ASPIER [38] abstracts C code into a model that it checks for a bounded number of sessions, and Kobeissi et al. [67] verified a JavaScript implementation of a Signal variant by translating it to ProVerif and CryptoVerif models.

Notably, another line of work annotates the source code itself with specifications and proves them with a type checker or program verifier. Arquint et al. [15] verify annotated Go and Java implementations against a Tamarin model, with a soundness argument that maps model terms to bytes; we follow their concretization in our symbolic refinement. Their main case study gives an end-to-end symbolically verified implementation of the WireGuard key exchange, derived from the official Go implementation of this widely deployed VPN and interoperable with it. To make verification tractable, they modified that code: they removed DDoS protection, metrics and load balancing, and adapted it around stubs for cryptographic and network operations. We verify the libsignal code unmodified. Dupressoir et al. [50] prove protocol properties of annotated C code with a general-purpose verifier.

All of these work either on the source level, on code written or modified for verification, on code in a verification-friendly language, or with a model extracted from source, so the guarantee for the running program relies on a trusted compiler, extraction step or language semantics. We verify the unmodified production library as it is compiled by the stock Rust compiler in a CLI harness (with hooked cryptographic primitives), and state our theorems over machine code. This removes the compiler and the Rust semantics from the trusted base, at the price of reasoning about optimized AArch64.

Mechanized symbolic model cryptography. Symbolic analyses make idealized assumptions about the underlying cryptographic primitives and model the attacker as a Dolev–Yao network adversary that manipulates messages as terms [49]. This focuses the analysis on the protocol design rather than the cryptographic algorithms employed by the protocol. In ProVerif [30, 32], protocols are specified in an applied pi-calculus (process calculus), and proofs are done by translation into Horn clauses, and attacker knowledge is represented as a predicate over these clauses. It permits reasoning about an unbounded number of sessions, but false positives are possible. Tamarin [76, 86] models state as multisets, protocols as multiset rewrite rules, and attacker knowledge as one kind of fact over multisets. Properties are stated in first-order logic over traces. Proofs are solved by constraint solving either automatically or auto-actively. DY⋆^\star⋆ [24] proves trace invariants of executable protocol code in F⋆^\star⋆, and two recent Lean frameworks build on its approach: DyLean [99], which adds user-defined equational theories and threat models, and LeanDY [63], which combines type-based and trace-based reasoning. Our symbolic specifications and proofs use DyLean, so the protocol model, its security proofs and the AArch64 semantics live in one logic, and Lean’s kernel checks the refinement between them.

Mechanized computational cryptography. Game-based proofs [88, 22] have been mechanized in CertiCrypt [18], EasyCrypt [17], FCF [81], CryptHOL [19] and SSProve [1], among others, and CryptoVerif [31] automates such proofs. Our development builds on VCVio [97], a library for oracle computations in Lean. These frameworks handle the efficiency of reductions in different ways. Some leave it informal, and others restrict reductions syntactically. We write reductions in a small costed language and prove explicit cost bounds (§5.2.2).

Verified cryptographic code. Verified implementations of cryptographic primitives (as opposed to protocols) are complementary to our work, since they specify and verify functional correctness properties (and sometimes constant-time execution) of the primitives that we use in our verification of a cryptographic protocol. Many prior works have verified these primitives, at the C or assembly level, including HACL⋆^\star⋆ [108], Fiat Cryptography [51], Vale [34], Jasmin [4], the formally verified ML-KEM in libcrux [44], and the s2n-bignum and AWS-LC proofs in HOL Light [8]. Computational security proofs of cryptographic primitives have been carried down to assembly through verified compilers [5, 6, 3]. To our knowledge, ours are the first proofs of protocol-level security properties for the unmodified code of a widely deployed implementation of a cryptographic protocol.

Verifying code at the binary level. Our AArch64 semantics belongs to a line of work on formal ISA models, including Sail [14], which we test against, Islaris [85], which verifies machine code against such models, and LNSym [55], an Armv8 symbolic simulator in Lean 4. CompCert [73] and the translation validation of seL4 [87] address the gap between source and machine code by verifying the compiler or each compilation. Neither is available for Rust, and source-level Rust verifiers such as hax [25], Aeneas [58] and Verus [71] trust rustc, LLVM and a model of Rust’s semantics, so we verify the compiler’s output directly. Ironclad Apps [57] proved end-to-end security properties of applications at the assembly level, but for applications written in Dafny for verification.

AI for formal verification. Language models have been extensively used to generate formal proofs over the last few years, in both mathematics [82, 103, 62, 96] and software verification. Some efforts in the latter category generate proof annotations in verification-aware languages like Dafny, Verus and F⋆^\star⋆ [100, 92, 102, 39]. Others focus on automatically discharging proof obligations for interactive provers [94, 106, 53].

AI capabilities in this area are growing rapidly. In 2025, an agent completed a formalization of the strong prime number theorem in about 25,000 lines of Lean [75]. In September 2026, a multi-agent AI system formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in about 13 million lines [9]. In software verification, AI systems have been primarily evaluated on the verification of small individual programs [93, 104], though there is early work on repository-level verification [101].

A number of recent efforts, carried out concurrently with this effort, have highlighted the ability of AI to scale up verification to cover compiled machine code. This includes MachCSL, which verifies the xv6 OS kernel against RISC-V privileged hardware semantics [65], verification of open-source fuzz targets compiled to RISC-V [11], and Zellic’s work on verifying glibc’s startup on x86 [105]. These efforts largely target generic properties, such as crash freedom, or functional correctness. By contrast, our work shows that verifying security of a complex deployed system requires sophisticated specifications, which are substantial engineering projects in their own right. This is why AlphaProof Code supports AI-assisted specification discovery as well as autonomous proof.

9 Discussion

We have introduced AlphaProof Code, a framework in which humans and AI agents collaborate on the formal specification and verification of software, and used it to prove the security of libsignal, the Signal protocol’s reference implementation, at the machine-code level. Our security proofs cover both the symbolic and the computational models. While there is a long line of prior work on formal verification of cryptographic protocols [32, 76, 17, 43, 28, 40, 27, 67], ours are the first proofs of protocol-level security properties for the unmodified code of a widely deployed implementation of a cryptographic protocol.

Our results can be extended in at least three directions. First, the theorems can be strengthened. Our computational theorem is classical, and our ratchet theorems let the attacker choose SPQR’s keys, so neither proves the post-quantum healing that SPQR is designed to provide. The model choices of §5.2.5 and §5.1.6, such as a single session per handshake and fixed message lengths, can be relaxed. Second, the trusted base can be reduced. The two output functions and a few library routines are trusted contracts; verifying them would move the trust boundary down to the system calls. The low-level cryptographic routines have idealized contracts, which could be connected to verified implementations [108, 44]. Third, the scope can be expanded beyond one-to-one sessions, for example, to Signal’s group messaging, sealed sender and server-side protocols.

More generally, our work is one of several recent efforts [11, 65] that point to a shift in the level of abstraction at which code is verified. The attraction of machine-code-level verification is that one needs to trust less—there is no need to model the semantics of high-level languages like Rust and C++ or assume that the compiler is correct. However, proofs at this level are long; when humans wrote almost all formal proofs, they were impractical beyond restricted domains. AI changes this equation by drastically reducing the labor cost of formal proof. That said, verifying at the source level remains a worthwhile way to reduce the compute cost of proof. For example, a substantial fraction of our proofs concerns registers, stack frames and memory layout, which source-level abstractions would hide. Extending our methods to higher-level languages would lower this cost, at the price of trusting the compiler and the language semantics, or of verifying them as well [73, 87].

One lesson is that while proofs are now much cheaper, specifications remain hard. The specification of a nontrivial software artifact is itself a nontrivial software artifact. Developing the software engineering discipline around formal specification is likely to become a fruitful area of research—conceptual frameworks, interfaces, and workflows through which humans and agents develop and validate a formal definition of what correctness and security mean. The process of §7, in which agents draft, review and test specifications under human direction, is a glimpse of how humans and AI might share this work. Like many of the most important problems in software engineering, this is a socio-technical challenge. Specifications of widely deployed systems need to be agreed upon by the communities that maintain, analyze and rely on them. Complex specifications, such as ours, will take many rounds of open review and refinement to settle. We are open-sourcing all Lean specifications and proofs, to facilitate such a process.

In the longer run, we expect AI-driven specification and verification to be tightly coupled with AI-driven coding. Today, verification happens after the code is written, if at all. Once every piece of code comes with a formal specification, and AI proofs are cheap, every change to the code can be verified before it is merged. AlphaProof Code extends naturally to this setting. It treats the specification as a living artifact, revised through reviewed amendments when proofs reveal that it is wrong (§2.3); code changes can be handled the same way, with groups of prover agents repairing the proofs that are affected when the code and (in many cases) the specification change. We are keen to use this workflow to verify new releases of libsignal before they ship, and also more broadly, as well. The coupling of code generation, specification and verification through AI could at last make machine-checked proofs of correctness and security routine for critical systems.

A The Signal Protocol in Detail

This appendix gives the details of PQXDH and the Triple Ratchet that §3 omits (Figure 8).

PQXDH. Each party has a long-term X25519 identity key IK\mathit{IK}IK. Bob uploads to the server a prekey bundle: a signed prekey SPKB\mathit{SPK}_BSPKB​ and a Kyber1024 prekey PQPKB\mathit{PQPK}_BPQPKB​ (single-use, or a reusable last-resort key), both signed with IKB\mathit{IK}_BIKB​ (XEdDSA), and optionally single-use one-time prekeys OPKB\mathit{OPK}_BOPKB​. Alice fetches the bundle, verifies the signatures, generates an ephemeral key EKA\mathit{EK}_AEKA​ and computes DH1=DH(IKA,SPKB)\mathit{DH}_1=\mathsf{DH}(\mathit{IK}_A,\mathit{SPK}_B)DH1​=DH(IKA​,SPKB​), DH2=DH(EKA,IKB)\mathit{DH}_2=\mathsf{DH}(\mathit{EK}_A,\mathit{IK}_B)DH2​=DH(EKA​,IKB​), DH3=DH(EKA,SPKB)\mathit{DH}_3=\mathsf{DH}(\mathit{EK}_A,\mathit{SPK}_B)DH3​=DH(EKA​,SPKB​) and, if a one-time prekey was used, DH4=DH(EKA,OPKB)\mathit{DH}_4=\mathsf{DH}(\mathit{EK}_A,\mathit{OPK}_B)DH4​=DH(EKA​,OPKB​). She encapsulates a secret ss\mathit{ss}ss to PQPKB\mathit{PQPK}_BPQPKB​, obtaining a ciphertext ct\mathit{ct}ct, and derives the session secret SK\mathit{SK}SK with HKDF from the DH values and ss\mathit{ss}ss. The DH values implicitly authenticate the parties, since only the holders of the identity keys can compute them, and ss\mathit{ss}ss protects SK\mathit{SK}SK against an adversary who records the handshake and later breaks Diffie-Hellman. Her first message, a PreKeySignalMessage, carries IKA\mathit{IK}_AIKA​, EKA\mathit{EK}_AEKA​, ct\mathit{ct}ct and the prekey identifiers together with her first encrypted message. Bob recomputes SK\mathit{SK}SK and deletes the one-time prekey.

The Triple Ratchet. SK\mathit{SK}SK is split into a root key, a chain key and a seed for SPQR. In the Double Ratchet [80], the symmetric ratchet derives each message key and the next chain key from the current chain key with HMAC-SHA256, so old keys can be deleted (forward secrecy). Each message carries the sender’s ratchet public key, and a party that sees a new one mixes a fresh DH output into the root key, so an adversary who has compromised a party’s state loses access after the next round trip, provided it does not interfere with that round trip (post-compromise security). This healing holds only against classical adversaries, so the Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet (SPQR) [89] runs an ML-KEM-768 exchange alongside, with keys and ciphertexts split into chunks carried in ordinary messages; each completed exchange yields an epoch key from which SPQR derives a key per message. The key that protects a message is derived from both the Double Ratchet’s and SPQR’s message keys. The message is encrypted with AES-256-CBC and authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 8 bytes, over both identity keys and the protobuf-encoded SignalMessage, which carries the sender’s ratchet key, counters for out-of-order delivery, the SPQR chunk and the ciphertext. The receiver keeps a bounded number of keys of skipped messages.

B Symbolic Proofs

This appendix completes §5.1: the composed model as a transition system (§B.1), the hardware events (§B.2), the concretization function (§B.3), explanations (§B.4), the collision clause (§B.5), the security statement and the scope of the binary theorem (§B.6, §B.7), and the preservation proof (§B.8).

B.1 The Composed Model

Each of the four libsignal entry points corresponds to one atomic transition in DyLean’s Traceful monad (so the DH and SPQR ratchets execute atomically inside messageDecrypt, never exposing a half-ratcheted state). Transitions read from and append to a single global append-only trace (ExecTrace), recording fresh randomness (genRand), network transmissions (sendMessage), immutable session-state snapshots referenced by trace handles (storeLocalState), and protocol events (logEvent). Compromises, exposures and breaks are protocol events (such as CompromisedIK, ExposedRK and BrokenDH); a compromise or exposure then sends the leaked secret on the network. Table 3 summarizes all 23 transitions of the composed state machine (ReachabilityConfig), which store long-term and prekey secrets (PQXDHState) as well as session snapshots (TRState) on the trace; any transition may fire at any time on attacker-chosen arguments whose guards hold.

B.2 Hardware Events Lean: RunEvent Lean: EnvEvent

A hardware trace is a list of events (CliEvents). A run event holds the party, the command, the run’s input, its coins, and its exit code with its standard output. The attacker may invert a key only after the matching break, and only a key that an honest party generated: a key of the setup, or one that a successful run drew from its coins. Table 4 lists every event.

B.3 Concretization Lean: gamma

γ\gammaγ (§5.1.4) is defined by recursion on terms: each function symbol fff comes with a function on byte strings, and γ(f(t1,…,tk))\gamma(f(t_1,\ldots,t_k))γ(f(t1​,…,tk​)) applies it to γ(t1),…,γ(tk)\gamma(t_1),\ldots,\gamma(t_k)γ(t1​),…,γ(tk​).

Literals stand for their own bytes, concat appends, trunc8 keeps the first 8 bytes, and the wire-message symbols give libsignal’s protobuf encoding. The cryptographic symbols use an interpretation I\mathcal{I}I, which gives each symbol’s result on its argument bytes. dhPk and dh are X25519, symEnc is AES-256-CBC, Encap is Kyber1024 encapsulation, and kdfExtract is HMAC-SHA256, built in Lean from the SHA-256 compression function. Among the laws assumed of I\mathcal{I}I is Diffie-Hellman commutativity: dh sorts its two secrets, so both parties compute the same shared-secret term, and commutativity gives them the same bytes. The remaining laws state that X25519 public keys are canonical and never low-order, that agreement reads only the u-coordinate, ignores torsion points and is zero exactly on low-order points, that the binary’s torsion check rejects a public key shifted by a torsion point (without this law the theorem is false, since the MAC does not cover the base key), that AES-CBC decryption inverts encryption and has no junk (a ciphertext that decrypts is the encryption of its plaintext), and that X25519 outputs and libcrux HMAC tags are 32 bytes long. These laws are trusted; we prove only that they are jointly satisfiable.

Lean definition: symEnc

classDY.SymEnc.CanSymEnc Symbolic.Specifications.Model.EquationalTheory.SymEnc (L26–29) →

public class CanSymEnc (Bytes: Type u) where symEnc: (key: Bytes) → (iv: Bytes) → (msg: Bytes) → Bytes symDec: (key: Bytes) → (iv: Bytes) → (ct: Bytes) → Err Bytes

Two more parameters complete γ\gammaγ. Some symbols are opaque: the SPQR operations, Kyber1024 public keys, decapsulation of a ciphertext that is not an honest encapsulation, and XEdDSA. Their bytes come from fixed byte functions SSS, which must agree with the setup: they give the setup’s signatures and Kyber public key their provisioned bytes, and decapsulation under Bob’s Kyber prekey agrees with I\mathcal{I}I. Nothing else is assumed about them. A per-trace ghost ggg gives the bytes of each fresh value: those of the piece of a run’s coins, or of the plaintext of a send run, that it is matched with, or, for the setup’s keys, the setup’s bytes. It also gives the bytes of each wire message’s addresses field, which has no model term. The ghost is the only part of γ\gammaγ that depends on the execution.

B.4 Explanations Lean: MatchesEvents Lean: Explains

Each transition along a model trace (§5.1.1) corresponds to at most one event from Table 4, carrying symbolic terms rather than bytes: for example, encrypting a message corresponds to a send run whose input is a fresh plaintext term, whose coins are fresh coins, and whose output is a wire-message term; compromising a secret corresponds to a leak; and a rejected run leaves the model state unchanged. A model trace matches a hardware trace τ\tauτ if these events line up with τ\tauτ’s events one to one, in order, and each byte field of a hardware event equals γ\gammaγ applied to the corresponding model term(s) under libsignal’s wire and key encodings.

A model trace explains τ\tauτ if it is reachable in the model, matches τ\tauτ, and agrees with the execution on details that the hardware events do not record. Because τ\tauτ records only what goes into and out of each run, it omits how stored session records overwrite prior state from run to run, and how incoming bytes were decoded and routed internally. Pinning explanations to these unlogged details prevents the model trace from reusing replaced session state or logging handshakes the binary did not perform when we evaluate the security queries on it, and—in the collision clause below—rules out degenerate explanations of a trace prefix.

B.5 The Collision Clause

The collision clause of the refinement definition (§5.1.4) excuses only runs that no explanation can account for without a collision between two different terms, at least one built by a symbol assumed injective. No opaque symbol is assumed injective. Two further clauses concern the truncated MAC: a received message is also excused if its 8-byte MAC equals one that the receiver computes from a ratchet seed the attacker does not know (a guessed MAC), or one computed under a different seed. Three features constrain the collision case. First, SSS is chosen before the hardware trace, and opaque bytes are never assumed injective, so SSS cannot be tuned to create collisions. Second, for a received message the collision must occur under every explanation of the prefix that has not already read a colliding message (except in the Kyber case below), so the proof cannot pick an explanation that happens to collide. Third, a received message counts as a collision only if every term the attacker knows that the model would accept for it itself involves a collision: once the attacker has leaked or inverted a key, a message it forges with that key must be explained, not excused.

One further clause concerns Kyber: a decapsulation that disagrees with encapsulation is excused, since no Kyber correctness law is assumed on I\mathcal{I}I; hardware traces in this case get no guarantee. The clause reads only the interpretation I\mathcal{I}I, the setup and the received ciphertext, never SSS, the ghost or the run, so it holds only if decapsulation under Bob’s provisioned key disagrees with encapsulation on that ciphertext: the hooked Kyber implementation is incorrect, the provisioned key is malformed (key generation is not verified, and well-formedness checks only the public key embedded in the secret key), or the ciphertext is one of the decryption failures that Kyber1024 has with negligible probability. (Kyber’s implicit rejection of a malformed ciphertext is modeled directly in the symbolic KEM by a secret-keyed rejection symbol, so it is explained rather than excused.)

B.6 The Security Statement

For initiator secrecy, for instance, the query in Q(tr,K)Q(\mathit{tr}, K)Q(tr,K) says that if Alice completed a handshake in tr\mathit{tr}tr and one of its keys is in KKK, then one of that row’s excuses of Table 5 holds on tr\mathit{tr}tr. The ten properties differ only in QQQ, where each is one conjunct: stated alone, each has exactly the shape of Theorem 1 with its own query in place of QQQ, and Theorem 1 implies all ten of these statements, with one common SSS, because QQQ is their conjunction. Table 5 states every query using the event shorthands defined next (for the events of Table 3).

A handshake query fixes the session’s parties aaa (Alice) and bbb (Bob), its keys ikA\mathit{ikA}ikA, ikB\mathit{ikB}ikB, spk\mathit{spk}spk, pqpk\mathit{pqpk}pqpk, opk\mathit{opk}opk and outputs keys={rk,ck,pqr}\mathit{keys}=\{\mathit{rk},\mathit{ck},\mathit{pqr}\}keys={rk,ck,pqr}, and the index iii of Alice’s AliceDone or Bob’s BobDone event; Done\mathsf{Done}Done is either. IKA\mathsf{IK}_AIKA​, IKB\mathsf{IK}_BIKB​, SPK\mathsf{SPK}SPK, PQ\mathsf{PQ}PQ, OPK\mathsf{OPK}OPK are the compromise events of the session’s identity keys and prekeys, and DH\mathsf{DH}DH, KEM\mathsf{KEM}KEM the breaks. An event EEE alone means EEE is logged anywhere on tr\mathit{tr}tr; E<iE^{<i}E<i and E≤iE^{\le i}E≤i, before and at or before iii. Exp(k)\mathsf{Exp}(k)Exp(k) (SessionStateExposed) holds if block kkk itself was exposed from a session started with keys\mathit{keys}keys. For the ratchet, mmm is a used message seed with SPQR salt sss; ck⇝m\mathit{ck}\leadsto mck⇝m and rk⇝ck\mathit{rk}\leadsto\mathit{ck}rk⇝ck mean derivation by chain and root ratchet steps, and rk⪯rk′\mathit{rk}\preceq\mathit{rk}'rk⪯rk′ that rk′\mathit{rk}'rk′ descends from rk\mathit{rk}rk. C(x)C(x)C(x) (CompromisedKey) holds if xxx was exposed, or is a handshake’s initial rk\mathit{rk}rk or ck\mathit{ck}ck and every handshake deriving it is excused by initiator or responder secrecy, or is an honest DH ratchet secret and DH\mathsf{DH}DH holds.

B.7 Scope of the Binary Theorem

The hardware traces fix a narrower scenario than the model; on other traces the theorem says nothing. The main restrictions are as follows (the Lean statement adds technical conditions on file paths). Alice and Bob each run on one device, and each starts with the other’s identity key pinned. Bob has one signed prekey, one reusable last-resort Kyber prekey and at most one one-time prekey; one-time Kyber prekeys are not covered. Only Alice runs init, and only when she has no session; only Bob receives prekey messages. The bundle Alice receives carries Bob’s genuine identity key, signed prekey and Kyber prekey with their signatures (the unsigned one-time prekey is unconstrained), and received SPQR fields come from earlier honest messages. A leak reveals only Alice’s identity secret, Bob’s identity, signed-prekey and Kyber secrets, his one-time prekey while unused, and the keys of a party’s current session. Inputs are below 2322^{32}232 bytes (a prekey message’s inner message below 232−20482^{32}-2048232−2048), files below 2312^{31}231 bytes, coins files exactly 192, 64 and 32 bytes for init, send and recv, and there are fewer than 232−12^{32}-1232−1 sends. After Bob accepts a prekey message that does not match his current session, he makes no call until the environment deletes his session file. The theorem also assumes fresh coins (§5.1.5). Within this scenario the attacker schedules every run, controls the network, may delete a party’s session file, and may leak secrets and break DH and the KEM, as in the model.

B.8 Refinement Preservation

The preservation theorem is proved once, independently of the binary: for every predicate relating the hooks to I\mathcal{I}I and every run relation, the ten model theorems and the refinement definition of §5.1.4 imply the statement of Theorem 1. The machine code enters only through the refinement theorem, so a new build of libsignal-cli needs a new refinement proof but no new security proof.

The proof has two steps. First, every explaining model trace is reachable, so each model theorem applies to it. Second, every term that the hardware attacker derives under an explanation is known to the model attacker on the explaining trace. Only this second step takes real work: each leaked or inverted secret matches a model step that reveals it, and two kinds of terms need model invariants showing that they already reached the attacker: the ephemeral key and Kyber ciphertext that Alice’s binary resends in every prekey message while her prekey is pending, and Bob’s one-time prekey.

The queries then transfer because of their shape. Each one either ignores the attacker’s knowledge (authentication, peer authentication, KCI) or uses it only as a hypothesis (“if the attacker knows this key, then an excuse holds”), and every excuse is an event of the model trace, never a fact about knowledge. So an attacker that knows less cannot break a query. A query whose excuse read “the attacker knows kkk” would not transfer this way.

In the collision case, preservation still gives the ten queries on every explanation of the prefix before the colliding run, so a collision voids the guarantees only from that run on.

C Computational Proofs

This appendix gives the precise game (§C.1), the cost semantics of reductions (§C.2), the four lemmas (§C.3), the full main theorem and its proof (§C.4), and the assumptions and restrictions in detail (§C.5, §C.6). The remaining subsections list the premises on the primitives and the terms of the single-session bound.

C.1 The Composed Game

The challenger holds every party’s state (in the game on the executable, the party’s directory) and plays the server that distributes identity keys and prekeys. It also supplies the coins of every run, except that the adversary chooses the coins of sends.

The game is written once, as a generic game G(Σ)G(\Sigma)G(Σ) parameterized by a protocol interface Σ\SigmaΣ that supplies the handshake and ratchet steps. The oracles and the winning condition consult Σ\SigmaΣ only through these steps, for example to decide whether an injected message is accepted. We write G(ΣmodelH)G(\Sigma^H_{\mathrm{model}})G(ΣmodelH​) for the game whose interface is the byte-level model with handshake HHH, and G(Σbin)G(\Sigma_{\mathrm{bin}})G(Σbin​) for the game whose interface is runs of libsignal-cli. The advantage of AAA is 2 ∣Pr⁡[A wins]−12∣2\,|\Pr[A\text{ wins}]-\tfrac12|2∣Pr[A wins]−21​∣, written Advcomp(A)\mathsf{Adv}^{\mathrm{comp}}(A)Advcomp(A) in G(ΣmodelH)G(\Sigma^H_{\mathrm{model}})G(ΣmodelH​) and Advbin(A)\mathsf{Adv}^{\mathrm{bin}}(A)Advbin(A) in G(Σbin)G(\Sigma_{\mathrm{bin}})G(Σbin​). In the main text, Advcomp\mathsf{Adv}^{\mathrm{comp}}Advcomp refers to H=HlibH=H_{\mathrm{lib}}H=Hlib​.

Handshake oracles. These are the oracles of the PQXDH key-indistinguishability game of [52]: registration of honest parties and of adversarial keys (whose secret keys the adversary must supply), generation of signed and one-time prekeys, initiation and acceptance, corruption of identity keys, reveal of session keys and of signed-prekey secrets, and, if the handshake models the session-key HKDF as a random oracle, queries to that oracle. The handshake itself is a parameter HHH.

Promotion. The test query of the key-indistinguishability game is withheld from the adversary. Instead, the adversary may promote an initiator session sidsidsid by calling startDR(sid)\mathsf{startDR}(sid)startDR(sid). The oracle checks that sidsidsid was initiated through the game and not yet promoted. It checks that sidsidsid used, byte for byte, the identity key, signed prekey, Kyber prekey and (if any) one-time prekey that a registered party published, with matching prekey identifiers, and that no earlier instance used the same ephemeral key. If so, it initializes the next ratchet instance, including SPQR, for both parties with the real session key. Finally, it marks the responder’s signed prekey used in the handshake as revealed in the handshake game; the secret goes to the ratchet, not to the adversary.

Ratchet oracles. Each ratchet instance has the oracles of the ACD19 secure-messaging game [7]: transmit, challenge (m0,m1)(m_0,m_1)(m0​,m1​), deliver, inject (a forgery attempt) and corruption of either party’s state. The adversary wins if it guesses the challenge bit bbb or gets a non-trivial forgery accepted, subject to ACD19’s cleanness conditions and the further restrictions of §C.6. If at the end the handshake part of the execution violates the freshness condition of [52], the game outputs a random bit.

SPQR. The ratchet in each session is libsignal’s Triple Ratchet: the Double Ratchet together with SPQR. SPQR carries ML-KEM-768 exchanges in chunks inside the message headers and, as they complete, outputs fresh 32-byte keys. Each message key is derived from the Double Ratchet’s chain key with the current SPQR key as the HKDF salt. SPQR lives in the protocol interface, not in the oracles, but the oracles reach it in four ways:

  • startDR\mathsf{startDR}startDR derives SPQR’s initial secret from the handshake key, along with the Double Ratchet’s;

  • adversarially chosen send coins are also SPQR’s coins, including those for ML-KEM key generation and encapsulation;

  • corrupting a party leaks its SPQR state with the rest of its ratchet state;

  • injected messages may carry arbitrary SPQR headers.

Handshakes. Both HlibH_{\mathrm{lib}}Hlib​ and HroH_{\mathrm{ro}}Hro​ are one-key handshakes with Kyber1024 (round 3) as the KEM. Prior analyses [52, 28] give each party two independent identity keys, one for Diffie-Hellman and one for signing. Standalone Lean proofs for that two-key model, and for its first-message authentication game, are preserved outside the trusted base.

Budgets. As in [52], the handshake budgets are per party. Each of at most NidN_{\mathrm{id}}Nid​ honest parties publishes a bounded number of signed-prekey bundles, each bundle a bounded number of one-time prekeys and of sessions accepted with and without one, and each party initiates a bounded number of sessions with and without a one-time prekey. We write NspkN_{\mathrm{spk}}Nspk​, NopkN_{\mathrm{opk}}Nopk​, NsendN_{\mathrm{send}}Nsend​ and NaccN_{\mathrm{acc}}Nacc​ for the resulting totals of signed prekeys, one-time prekeys, initiated sessions and accepted sessions, Nsend,opk\leNsendN_{\mathrm{send,opk}}\leN_{\mathrm{send}}Nsend,opk​\leNsend​ for the initiated sessions that use a one-time prekey, and Ndh=Nid+Nspk+Nopk+NsendN_{\mathrm{dh}}=N_{\mathrm{id}}+N_{\mathrm{spk}}+N_{\mathrm{opk}}+N_{\mathrm{send}}Ndh​=Nid​+Nspk​+Nopk​+Nsend​ for the number of X25519 key pairs that the challenger generates. The adversary makes at most qhsq_{\mathrm{hs}}qhs​ handshake queries in total, of which at most qonq_{\mathrm{on}}qon​ are not random-oracle queries (with separate caps on random-oracle queries), and qstartq_{\mathrm{start}}qstart​ promotions. The kkk-th promoted session allows at most qkq_kqk​ ratchet queries, where 2(qk+1)+25002<2322(q_k+1)+25002<2^{32}2(qk​+1)+25002<232, and qepq_{\mathrm{ep}}qep​ epochs (ACD19’s epoch cap).

C.2 Reductions and Their Costs

A reduction RRR runs the adversary AAA exactly once, as a black box and without rewinding. It prepares AAA’s input, answers each of AAA’s oracle queries by running a handler, and computes its own output from AAA’s. A handler may compute on ordinary data (numbers, lists, tables), sample uniform coins and query the oracles of the assumption game. It operates on keys and group elements only through declared primitive operations, and it loops only up to a bound written in the program. If the assumption game has a challenge phase, RRR may also pause AAA at one query, send a value to the game, and resume the same run of AAA with the game’s answer.

Costs are computed from the program text alone. Primitive operations, samples and oracle queries are charged from a fixed table per primitive. The cost of RRR against an adversary that makes qqq game queries is

cost(R,q)  =  cinit+q⋅max⁡(ccoin, chandle+ccodec)+cfinish,\mathrm{cost}(R,q) \;=\; c_{\mathrm{init}} + q\cdot\max(c_{\mathrm{coin}},\,c_{\mathrm{handle}}+c_{\mathrm{codec}}) + c_{\mathrm{finish}},cost(R,q)=cinit​+q⋅max(ccoin​,chandle​+ccodec​)+cfinish​,

the syntactic costs of setup, of forwarding a coin or answering one query (including its encoding), and of the output step. For reductions that pause AAA, the handlers before and after the pause, and the pause step itself, enter through maxima. The cost bounds RRR’s work outside AAA, and a similar count, made syntactically or stated over the run, bounds RRR’s queries to the assumption oracles. RRR is cost-bounded if three conditions hold. First, its cost and its query count are bounded by explicit polynomials in the game’s budgets, independent of AAA. Second, no primitive operation or sample produces values larger than its declared cost allows, so that unit costs cannot hide large data; hence, on every run in which AAA’s queries and the oracle answers have bounded size, all values that RRR computes have bounded size too. Third, its program has at most 224+212(⌊log⁡2b⌋+1)2^{24}+2^{12}(\lfloor\log_2 b\rfloor+1)224+212(⌊log2​b⌋+1) nodes, where bbb is its cost budget, so that RRR cannot carry a large table, such as a table of discrete logarithms. A few fixed wrappers in our statements lie outside this language (§C.6). They are part of the trusted base.

The lazy-sampling condition concerns HHH together with the game’s driver. Fix k<qstartk<q_{\mathrm{start}}k<qstart​ and a bit bkb_kbk​, and consider the hybrid in which ratchet instances i<ki<ki<k use challenge bit 1, instance kkk uses bit bkb_kbk​ and instances i>ki>ki>k use bit 0, run against HHH in the random-key world. The condition requires that this hybrid has the same output distribution whether instance kkk is keyed with the key derived from HHH’s test answer or with a fresh uniform key. A condition on HHH alone (“a fresh key in place of one tested key is invisible”) would fail for every partner-consistent handshake, since the adversary could test both partners. The driver withholds the test query and promotes at most one instance per ephemeral key. We prove the condition for HlibH_{\mathrm{lib}}Hlib​ for every adversary.

Lemma 4 concerns the machine code. Let enc\mathsf{enc}enc encode a model state as a party’s directory (the files of Figure 4, with each session stored as libsignal’s serialized record), and let obs\mathsf{obs}obs map a model outcome to an exit code, a standard output and new file contents. A party state σ\sigmaσ is well-formed if its session, if any, is one reachable from a PQXDH handshake followed by ratchet steps, every file of enc(σ)\mathsf{enc}(\sigma)enc(σ) is below 2312^{31}231 bytes, and its prekey identifiers of each kind are distinct. “No terminal state” is an outcome that the model never produces, so clause 1 includes termination. A rejected operation exits with code 1 and writes no file. The exception arises because, when it accepts such a message, libsignal archives the old session in the new record, which our encoding does not represent. The game never reaches the accepted case: the initiator refuses every prekey message, and the responder accepts one over an existing session only if its header is that of the session’s handshake. The lemma assumes nothing about the hooked primitives. That the real routines behave as their Lean specifications is part of the trusted base (§5.3). The lemma is functional refinement of whole runs, and intermediate machine states are unconstrained. For SPQR, step\mathsf{step}step uses our Lean model of spqr 1.6.0, which is trusted. The lemma fixes every output, including on rejected and adversarial inputs, so any deviation from the model, harmful or not, contradicts it, whether it comes from the Rust source or the compiler.

Proof outline. The proof is compositional, in a separation logic for AArch64. Each compiled function, including inlined Rust library code (Vec, protobuf, SessionRecord serialization, SPQR), the CLI’s argument handling and file-backed stores, and musl’s start-up and exit code and its mallocng allocator, gets a contract relating its registers and memory footprint to the corresponding model function. Contracts are proved by symbolic execution with a weakest-precondition calculus (callee contracts, hook specifications, loop invariants, the frame rule, and bit-vector side conditions proved in Lean’s kernel). Since the semantics is deterministic, the contract of the whole run determines its unique terminal state. □\square□

The challenger writes no session file, so every session record a party holds was written by its own run of the executable. Proof. The Lean proof combines Lemma 1, Lemma 4 and the no-out-of-memory theorem (§4.1), used through their statements, with a composition argument that follows Lemma 3 and Lemma 2 but is carried out directly, in a game that stops at the first ML-KEM-768 decryption failure. This is needed because the ML-KEM-768 term of Lemma 2 is evaluated on adversaries built by the composition reductions, which can trigger a failure with probability 1; the halted game charges the failure once, on AAA itself.

  1. Correctness of every run. By Lemma 4, every run in the game (init, the first prekey recv, and every later send and recv) has the model’s outcome unless the machine runs out of memory, which the no-out-of-memory theorem rules out. This includes the compiled spqr state machine, which computes what our Lean model of SPQR predicts. Only its ML-KEM-768 and HMAC routines are hooked (§4).

  2. Coupling. The binary game stores directories, and the model game stores model states. The coupling invariant is that every directory is enc(σ)\mathsf{enc}(\sigma)enc(σ) for the corresponding reachable σ\sigmaσ, and (i) preserves it at every oracle call. It breaks only if a Kyber1024 decapsulation in an honest handshake fails, which costs at most 2 NsendNspk δkem2\,N_{\mathrm{send}}N_{\mathrm{spk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kem}}2Nsend​Nspk​δkem​. Bound the advantage of A′A'A′ by the hybrid argument of Lemma 3 with H=HlibH=H_{\mathrm{lib}}H=Hlib​, whose lazy-sampling condition holds for every adversary, and each per-session term as in Lemma 2 with q=qkq=q_kq=qk​, in the game halted at the first ML-KEM-768 failure; reaching that failure costs at most 2 εmlkem(A)2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mlkem}}(A)2εmlkem​(A). C.5 Assumptions in Detail

Joint security. Because libsignal uses a single Curve25519 scalar per party for both X25519 Diffie-Hellman and XEdDSA bundle signatures [79], Lemma 1 pairs its signature and Diffie-Hellman games following standard joint-security definitions [46, 95]. XEdDSA EUF-CMA gives the adversary the X25519 decisional DH oracle (GapSigEufCma), and single-pair X25519 Gap-DH gives the adversary an XEdDSA signing oracle on the first challenge key (GapDhWithSign).

Outside the trusted base, we mechanize SHA-512 random-oracle reductions from both joint assumptions to standalone X25519 Gap-DH for libsignal’s randomized XEdDSA [95, 35, 97] under an abstract prime-order group-algebra witness (XeddsaCurveLaws, §C.10). These are a single-run reduction for GapDhWithSignRo with a factor-2 loss from guessing the Edwards sign bit, a two-run DDH-checked variant with factor 1, and a rewinding Forking-Lemma reduction for GapSigEufCmaRo with a 2(qH+1) AdvGapDH(B2)\sqrt{2(q_H+1)\,\mathsf{Adv}^{\mathrm{GapDH}}(B_2)}2(qH​+1)AdvGapDH(B2​)​ bound. Lemma 1 and Theorem 2 retain GapDhWithSign and GapSigEufCma directly, for three reasons: βKI\beta_{\mathsf{KI}}βKI​ avoids the square-root degradation of the Forking Lemma across NidN_{\mathrm{id}}Nid​ identities, each reduction in the theorem remains a single-run program in the costed language without rewinding, and the theorem avoids assuming a SHA-512 random oracle or concrete Curve25519/Ed25519 field arithmetic.

Environment. The statement assumes functional properties of the hooked ML-KEM-768, AES-256-CBC and X25519 routines, such as that decryption inverts encryption (§C.7 and §C.8). Everything else about the environment is part of the trusted base (§5.3):

  • the hooked routines of §4 (low-level cryptography, with AES-256-CBC including padding hooked as one function; error-message formatting; three libc memory and string routines, memmove, bcmp and strlen; the two functions that write files and standard output; and the remaining non-crypto Rust library routines) behave as their Lean specifications say, write only their declared outputs (no other caller-saved register), and fail only as specified (e.g., no full disk);

  • the clock reads the UNIX epoch;

  • each call is a fresh, non-setuid process at a fixed load address (no ASLR), with only standard input, output and error open, an empty environment, an 8 MiB stack, 1 GiB of available memory and fixed kernel random bytes (§4.1); and

  • spqr’s CPU-feature probe reports no AES or PMULL instructions, so the proofs follow the portable code paths.

C.6 Restrictions in Detail

Adversary and game. Besides the restrictions in §5.2.5, receive coins are honest, the responder does not send first in the first epoch, and injected ratchet keys must lie in the prime-order group. A few adversarial actions (revealing any signed-prekey secret, or corrupting the initiator’s identity key of any session before its responder accepts) make all later ratchet queries, in every session, return a default answer. Wins recorded before such an action still count, and the handshake test remains available. However, the theorem does not make claims about attacks that combine such an action with queries to an unrelated session. The handshake game is the variant of [52] with registered secret keys, no randomness reveals and a peer that is uncorrupted at session start. Smaller restrictions are listed in the artifact’s deviation log.

Setting. Budgets are fixed per instance. There is no self-session, and Bob’s Kyber prekey is always a last-resort key. With 8-byte MACs, the statistical terms are multiples of μ≥2−64\mu\ge 2^{-64}μ≥2−64 that grow polynomially in qkq_kqk​ and qepq_{\mathrm{ep}}qep​ (quadratically in each, per session, and summed over sessions; see §5.2.5 and §C.9).

Binary. Prekey messages are covered only in canonical protobuf encoding. The requirement of the promotion oracle that the bundle match published keys is argued, not mechanized, to lose no generality. The verified executable, on which both the computational and the symbolic theorems are stated, is built with rustc’s release profile with one codegen unit and panic=abort, linked statically with stock LLVM ld.lld (--no-relax) at fixed base address 0x400000 (with external linker resolution checked in CI by alink_check.py); each hooked routine is intercepted at entry by its contract (with libc memmove/bcmp/strlen and the two output routines linked from libc.a and libsignal-cli-io, and the remaining unlinked hooked routines and 18 panic entry points linked as four-byte zero stubs, which trap if executed unhooked). Each run starts with SPQR’s CPU-feature probe already set to report no AES or PMULL support, so SPQR takes its software code paths.

Cost model. The wrapper that refuses the corruptions the game forbids, and the glue that runs the reductions on the adversary, are plain Lean functions rather than programs in the reduction language; they are part of the trusted base. All other reductions in the statement, including the simulators for Figure 8 of ACD19, are cost-bounded.

C.7 Well-Formedness of the Handshake Primitives

Lemma 1 quantifies over primitives that satisfy the following conditions. They quantify over all inputs, in some cases restricted to canonical, on-curve or correctly sized ones as stated; in particular the adversary may supply any 32 bytes as an X25519 public key, including small-order and twist points. That the real primitives satisfy them is a trusted premise.

  • W1 Lengths and totality. Every primitive returns outputs of the expected byte lengths (hashes, AES blocks, X25519 values, scalars, Edwards points, Kyber1024 keys and ciphertexts), Kyber1024 encapsulation and decapsulation succeed on well-sized inputs, and SPQR initialization always succeeds.

  • W2 Agreement with reference definitions. SHA-512, the HKDF that derives the session key, the root and chain key derivations, message-key derivation, AES-256-CBC with HMAC, XEdDSA verification and the canonicity check on public keys agree with reference definitions written in Lean.

  • W3 Algebraic laws of X25519. X25519 is invariant under scalar clamping and commutes on base-point products; a product of the base point never yields the all-zero output; whether an output is all-zero does not depend on the scalar; the base point is canonical and canonical inputs give canonical outputs; multiplication by the cofactor 8 commutes with X25519; the signing public key is the X25519 public key; and the Gap-DH oracle agrees with its reference predicate, is symmetric, and is consistent with X25519 in either argument.

  • W4 Cofactor projection. The projection onto the prime-order subgroup is idempotent; X25519 outputs depend on a public key only through its projection, and conversely equal outputs under one scalar imply equal projections; scalars with the same public key agree on every on-curve input; the projection is injective on canonical keys; and only 32-byte strings project onto the projection of a public key.

  • W5 Correctness. AES-256 block decryption inverts encryption, the AEAD decrypts what it encrypts, XEdDSA signatures verify, and SPQR’s initial send state has a matching receive state with the same salt; every salt SPQR’s receive initialization produces, on any input, has at most 32 bytes.

  • W6 Key collisions. A fresh X25519 public key has the same projection as a given one with probability at most 2−2502^{-250}2−250, and a fresh Kyber1024 public key equals a given one with probability at most 2−2552^{-255}2−255. (The bound 2−2502^{-250}2−250 rather than 2−2512^{-251}2−251 is tight for clamped scalars. The bound 2−2552^{-255}2−255 rather than 2−2562^{-256}2−256 is needed because the Kyber1024 public key depends only on the 32-byte seed ddd, through G=SHA3-512G=\mathrm{SHA3\text{-}512}G=SHA3-512. If GGG is a random function, some two of the 22562^{256}2256 seeds collide with probability 1−e−1/2≈0.391-e^{-1/2}\approx 0.391−e−1/2≈0.39, and then the bound 2−2562^{-256}2−256 per target key, a property of the fixed function GGG, fails; three seeds collide only with probability about 2−258.62^{-258.6}2−258.6, so the bound 2−2552^{-255}2−255 holds almost surely.) These give the two collision terms of βKI\beta_{\mathsf{KI}}βKI​.

Kyber1024’s decapsulation correctness is not among these conditions; it enters Lemma 1 separately, as the bound δkem\delta_{\mathrm{kem}}δkem​.

C.10 SHA-512 Random-Oracle Reductions for XEdDSA

Outside the trusted base, we mechanize SHA-512 random-oracle reductions from GapDhWithSign and GapSigEufCma to standalone X25519 Gap-DH modulo the cofactor 8 for libsignal’s randomized XEdDSA signer xeddsaSignRef [79, 95, 35]. Let

ℓ=2252+27742317777372353535851937790883648493\ell = 2^{252} + 27742317777372353535851937790883648493ℓ=2252+27742317777372353535851937790883648493

Model boundaries. Four boundaries separate these standalone reductions from Lemma 1 and Theorem 2: (a) §C.7 does not pin the primitive signing function to xeddsaSignRef, since libsignal-cli only verifies received bundle signatures; (b) XeddsaCurveLaws is not proved for concrete GF(2255−19)\mathrm{GF}(2^{255}-19)GF(2255−19) Curve25519/Ed25519 arithmetic, as curve25519-dalek lies outside the binary proof scope (§5.2.4); (c) the primitive bridge in the binary theorem instantiates SHA-512 as the concrete Merkle–Damgård hash function rather than a lazy random oracle; and (d) the 2(qH+1) AdvGapDH(B2)\sqrt{2(q_H+1)\,\mathsf{Adv}^{\mathrm{GapDH}}(B_2)}2(qH​+1)AdvGapDH(B2​)​ Forking-Lemma loss makes the signature reduction qualitative rather than concrete-tight at deployment budgets (Nid=220N_{\mathrm{id}}= 2^{20}Nid​=220, qH=264q_H = 2^{64}qH​=264).
